quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Well met, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. Would that we had the time for banter, but we're all up in arms here. Yet another Ixali dirigible has been spotted over the Twelveswood, you see.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: I say, you have the look of an archer about you, and a capable one at that. Ordinarily, I would extol to you the virtues of the Archers' Guild, but I'm afraid that'll have to wait. Yet another Ixali dirigible has been spotted over the Twelveswood, you see, and everyone is up in arms.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Their reappearance calls to my mind the Battle of Griffin Crossing. Well, I say “Battle”─most are agreed that “Massacre” is rather more apt. Aye, the Ixal dealt us a crushing defeat that day. Right around this time of year, it was, two decades past.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: A humiliating episode in our history, to be sure, but heavens forbid that we of the Gods' Quiver ever forget it. Failure is the finest─if not the kindest─of teachers, and few things drive a man better than its sting.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Ah, but do let's speak of cheerier matters. Mayhap you've already heard, but a renowned archer has recently returned to the Twelveswood─the one they call the Godsbow.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: That's just a title, of course. His birthname is Jehantel, and he was once of the Gods' Quiver. The man was a legend even then, and there was no honor greater than being taken under his tutelage.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: But that's not all there is to him, mind you. Jehantel was also a skilled bard, one of the rare few capable of inspiring others to great feats through song.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Alas, to our great loss, Jehantel took an arrow in the knee twenty summers past, and abruptly retired from our ranks. Rumors has it he then took up the life of a wandering bard, but wherever he has been, his absence from the Quiver's Hold has done naught to diminish his stature.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Upon learning that the Godsbow had returned, dozens of us flocked to him in hopes of training under a legend, yours truly included.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Alas, the meetings haven't unfolded quite as we had hoped. Jehantel has refused to teach each and every suitor that has approached him thus far.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: That is, unless you count poetry and song─he seemed exceedingly keen to teach us all about them. Some few of us were tempted to take him up on the offer...save that we have a nation to defend.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Far be it from my intent to belittle all those bards out there, but I like my chances rather better charging into battle with a bow rather than a harp. <sigh> And here we were hoping that transcendent mastery of the bow might be ours...

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Hm? By the sparkle in your eyes, I'd wager you have an interest in poetry and song. Come now, there is no call for shyness. If you would present yourself as a pupil to Jehantel, I happen to know his whereabouts.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: That's the spirit! Now, I'm given to understand that Jehantel has made his camp somewhere north of Camp Tranquil. He's an agreeable sort of fellow, and should be willing enough to meet with you.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Truth be told, I'm still holding on to hope. If you could find a way into Jehantel's confidence, mayhap he can yet be persuaded to train us. I wish you the best of luck, friend.

quest_names: A Song of Bards and Bowmen
A Song of Bards and Bowmen
text_en: Oh... Well, my mistake. It's just that, to look at you, I thought that mayhap─ N-Never mind.

Ah, that glint of determination in your eyes is testament to your newfound strength. You put me in mind of my salad days, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)].
Hm? You would know why I [@1A(1)]truly[@1A(0)] abandoned the battlefield and became a bard?
That I took an arrow in the knee is what most folk believe...but it is quite clear you are not “most folk.” Very well. I shan't insult your intelligence with an untruth.

For now, allow me to answer by saying that everything in creation is given to change, and man most of all. I was drawn to the power of song─the power to touch the very souls of men─and decided that I must pursue it.

Sadly, that power has been all but forgotten in this age of cynicism. Such songs as those performed by tavern bards serve no purpose beyond the amusement of drunkards. But that was not always the way of it. There was a time when song could shape the outcome of conflict.

Ever since nations first quarreled, armies have fielded archers wherewith they rained death upon the enemy from afar. As the battle unfolded, however, the distinction between the lines of friend and foe would grow hazy. Yet the archer's part did not end there.

He had to stay ever alert, with arrow nocked and eyes trained upon the struggle. Even as his comrades fell, turning the earth red with their blood, the archer could ill afford to avert his gaze, lest that moment cost another his life.
One need not have a vivid imagination to appreciate the torrent of emotions that rages within him in that moment.
Nerves near to fraying, his breast fit to burst, the archer did the only thing he could: he sang. His bow became a makeshift instrument, plucked as an accompaniment.

At first, the archer sang only to still the roiling within. But his voice chanced to carry to his comrades. It inspirited those engaged in combat, lending strength to their sword arms. And to those who lay upon the precipice of death, it granted a measure of peace.
Realizing the tactical potential of song, yet loath to set aside skilled archers for that purpose, armies began raising dedicated regiments of minstrels.
But the members of such units were no warriors, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)].
Fair of voice and nimble of finger, these career minstrels could find a place in the hall of any lord.
Yet they knew naught of the burden borne by those who charge into battle─whose lot is to dance with death and sup on pain. And so their songs rang hollow, holding no power over the hearts of men.

[@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. This lesson I have taught, I would have you experience with bow in hand. Only by tasting the solitude of one who has lost all he holds dear will a new melody be revealed to you.
Take yourself to the Nanawa Mines north of Ul'dah. There you will encounter a lone jackal known as Bardi.
The grizzled creature once stood proud as lord of its pack, but it has since been deposed by a younger, stronger male.

Though it is now condemned to live out its days as an exile, it still burns with the desire to protect its own─a desire which has driven it to the depths of savagery. By your arrow, I would have you end the misery of this fallen lord.
In facing this foe in mortal combat and understanding what drives it, the Soul of the Bard will surely find new expression through you.
Your opponent may be past its prime, but know that every old dog learned a trick or two in its youth, and gained a foul temper in the meantime. See that you are fully prepared for the encounter.
Take here this linkpearl, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], and let us speak again when your task is accomplished.
Heed me, O Puissant Althyk! Make of the proud oak a humble acorn, that we might gaze upon the battles of yore!

Until you learn to accept pain as your companion, you can never walk the path of the true bard. Reflect upon these words, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], and consult with your heart what it is you truly seek.
Your zeal is commendable, but you must grow stronger if the Soul of the Bard is to reveal a new melody to you. Return hither once you have passed more time in the midst of death.
The next bard quest will be available from Jehantel upon reaching level 35.

Make your way to the Central Shroud, where you must seek out and vanquish the boar named Phaia. In surviving this trial, a new melody will surely resound within your heart, and by its music I shall know of your readiness for the next stage of your journey.
Only then will I be satisfied that the lesson to be learned from the Ballad of the Vainglorious Fool will not be lost upon you.

'Tis good to see you return, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], and more seasoned still for your time in the world. Call me a spoony bard, but as a man in the winter of his years, it gives me great joy to observe an adventurer in the spring of [@IF($E9(4),hers,his)].

This is an odd time for recollection, but it was a spring day when a bard first came to my home town. He played the most sorrowful chords, even as his words tantalized the ear like the breath of one's first love. Many a maiden's heart was stolen during his visit...and doubtless more besides. Ah, but I do ramble.
[@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. Would you believe that common bards, too, were born of archers? This may seem far-fetched upon first hearing, but it isn't so far a stretch.

Ask yourself this: what becomes of soldiers when conflict gives way to peacetime? Some have lives they might return to, aye, but most must needs take up a new trade to make ends meet. Well, it so happened that many who had once bent the bow took to strumming the harp.

They wandered the realm, singing passionately and earnestly of the war as seen through their own eyes─of sweet victories and bitter defeats, of sacrifice and cowardice. Their songs so captured the imagination of the people, nary a day passed that a bard was not called to perform, be it in a humble tavern or some great lord's hall.
Alas, their popularity proved their downfall. Intoxicated by the attentions of the masses, the bards took to embellishing their songs in a bid to outdo one another.
And over time, each song was shorn of verity, till the bard's repertoire contained not one shred of truth.

By now you will know that such songs have no purchase upon men's hearts. Certainly, a bawdy tune may set off fits of laughter in a sailor, and a sorrowful ballad summon tears from the eyes of a soft-hearted maiden. Yet these are but pale shadows of what songs can achieve.
For a blessing, this decline did not escape the notice of the moogles. As great patrons of the arts, they feared that the true power of song might be lost to mankind.
So it was that they labored to gather and safeguard those crystals known as Souls of the Bard, that they might be bestowed upon worthy men and women.

Now, well as I know you relish listening to my sermons, I daresay it's past time we moved on to the practical side of the lesson. Tell me, young one, are you perchance familiar with the Ballad of the Vainglorious Fool?
Nay? Well, that won't do at all. We must remedy this posthaste.
The song recounts the Massacre of Griffin Crossing, a battle that took place decades past, wherein countless Gridanian lives came to a premature end.

Ah, but do forgive me─I seem to have mistaken the proper order of things. Before I begin, I must be convinced that the point of the tale will not be lost upon you. Elsewise I will have wasted my breath in the telling of it.

Now, heed well these instructions. You must make your way to the Central Shroud, where you are to seek out and vanquish the boar named Phaia. But be forewarned: arrows are as needles to its thick hide.

In order to prevail over such an adversary, you must needs identify its weakness. For this you will require such focus as only comes with a tranquil heart, and the fortitude with which to maintain it in the face of fear.
In surviving this trial, a new melody will surely resound within your heart, and by its music I shall know of your readiness for the next stage of your journey.
Only then will I be satisfied that the lesson to be learned from the Ballad of the Vainglorious Fool will not be lost upon you.
Heed me, O Puissant Althyk! Reverse Thee the roaring river's flow, that we might gaze upon the battles of yore!
It takes a courage of sorts to admit when something is beyond your capacity. Go then, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], and return hither once you have mustered the confidence to undertake this trial.

It is in the extremity of battle that we plumb unknown depths of emotion. There, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], is where you will come upon your next melody. I shall be here, should you have a mind to recount your exploits.

North of Hyrstmill is where I would have you escort me, young one.
You may depart as soon as you are able─I shall follow apace. I look forward to witnessing your progress firsthand.
The next bard quest from Jehantel is now available.
Welcome back, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. By your tranquil countenance, it is plain that both your body and soul are in readiness for the next stage of your journey.
Very well. The time is ripe that I teach you the Ballad of the Vainglorious Fool.
The song tells the tale of an archer of the Gods' Quiver whose peerless skill was surpassed only by his hubris.
Alas, that hubris led to the annihilation of his entire regiment at the battle which has come to be called the Massacre of Griffin Crossing. Ahem!
Standing guard in dead of night,♪[@CR]An archer, wearying of the sight,♪[@CR]Drunk on pride and starved of glory,♪[@CR]Forsook his post to claim a victory.♪
Ten score yalms had the archer crept,♪[@CR]When shrieks rang out whence his comrades slept,♪[@CR]For he was not there to see the knives,♪[@CR]Nor to ring the bell and save friends' lives.♪
Tell me, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], what lessons can be learned from this tale?
Ah, but hold that thought─what your tongue claims to understand interests me not.
As before, I'd sooner have you demonstrate the fruits of your learning with bow in hand. This time, however, you shall have the pleasure of my company.
I would have you escort me to a place north of Hyrstmill, young one. There is something there that I long to see with mine own eyes.
That is well. You may depart as soon as you are able─I shall follow apace. I look forward to witnessing your progress firsthand.
Heed me, O Puissant Althyk! Cast Thee back the rains to the firmament, that we might gaze upon the battles of yore!
Mayhap the thought of my shadowing your every step discomfits you. Speak to me again once you have steeled your resolve.
It is well to have a strong heart, but without a fitting vessel to bear it, there is only so much one can achieve.
Once I deem your body and soul in harmony, I shall teach you the Ballad of the Vainglorious Fool.

Though you are my pupil, I suspect that I have learned more from you than you have from me. I am grateful to have met you, young one.
You are worthy of the choral attire, of this I am thoroughly convinced.
The markings I have made on your map shall guide you to each of the garments.
Go forth, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)], and claim that which is yours by rights.
It heartens me to see you again, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. I must apologize for having subjected you to danger.
With your permission, I would put the matter behind us. Let us focus instead upon the present. In your last lesson, I sang for you─this time I would have you sing for me.
A heartfelt performance, masterfully delivered.
You have come far in such a short time, my young apprentice.
Hearing your song this day, I am convinced that you are well on your way to surpassing me, as bard and archer both. Soon there will be naught left for me to impart to you.
[@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. You have proven yourself worthy of the consecrated garments worn by the true bards of old to honor the Keeper. I speak of the choral attire.

The attire was entrusted to me when Pukno Poki and I first met, deep within the Twelveswood. The moogle and I had traded scarce more than a handful of words when he proffered to me the attire along with the Soul of the Bard.

At that time, I knew not the true power of song, and so declined the gifts...but Pukno Poki would not be denied. For all his good humour, the moogle can be as unmoving as a rock. “The attire chooses the wearer, not the other way round,” he insisted, and I found myself yielding to his will.
In mastering the verses of war, I won acclaim beyond my wildest dreams upon the field of battle, and for a time I was well pleased.
Alas, my lust for glory knew no bounds, the consequence of which you are already aware.

It was in the wake of the Massacre of Griffin Crossing. Stricken with guilt, I wanted naught more than the earth to open up to swallow me whole. I had lost the will to live, aye, but I was too craven to end it myself.
And so I took to wandering aimlessly, in search of a place to die, far away from the judging eyes of men.

Disillusioned with the power of song, I committed an act of folly: I scattered the choral attire across the realm. “If truly the attire chooses its wearer,” I challenged, “then let it find its way back to me.”

Determined that I would not be proven wrong, I went to great pains to ensure that the attire would never again see the light of day, and the pieces now rest in places of peril. Being the proud fool that I was, it never crossed my mind that mayhap another was meant to don it.
I would entrust the choral attire to you, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. But as you can see, you must needs brave the dangers to claim it.
I shall mark its whereabouts on your map, but I can afford you no further aid beyond that. What say you, my young apprentice? Will you embark upon a journey to claim what is yours by rights?
I am deeply sorry that my folly of years past has entailed this burden upon you. But Althyk works in mysterious ways─in His wisdom, it may be that He has sent this trial to test your spirit.
I mean not for my sentiments to encumber you, but I am convinced that you are the one chosen by the choral attire.

But pray do not take that as license for complacency. Trials wouldn't be called such if they failed to tax one's ability. Stay ever on your toes, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. I would have you return whole of body, and bearing the garments.
Heed me, O Puissant Althyk! Reverse Thee the seasons' turning, that we might gaze upon the battles of yore!
I had ventured to hope that you were the one chosen by the attire. It casts me down to see that I was mistaken.

Well done, my young apprentice. In returning with the choral attire, you have reaffirmed my faith in you. For each thing I have taught you, you have repaid me twofold in joy. No teacher could ask for a better student.
Now then, there is a matter to which I must attend─something I have put off for long years for want of resolve. I shall share with you the details once I have made ready to depart.
The next bard quest will be available from Jehantel upon reaching level 50.
Your coming has instilled in me the resolve I need to confront my demons─something I have put off these many years. I am ready at last to make a pilgrimage to the scene of my regiment's demise.
Our destination is where the Griffin Crossing meets the central highlands of Coerthas. There, I shall honor my fallen comrades with song, in hopes that their tormented souls might be laid to rest.
Well done, my young apprentice. In returning with the choral attire, you have reaffirmed my faith in you.
I see no further reason to withhold from you the existence of the final piece in the set...the piece that has brought us together.

Listen well, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]. When I put down my bow, I vowed never again to set foot in the Twelveswood. That I now forsake my oath is for no other reason than to impart my knowledge to one who would succeed me.
Lest you wonder why I should deem that so important─permit me to relate to you an event which brought about a great change in me.
My most recent journey had taken me to Ul'dah, where I found myself ambling through the marketplace early one morn.
Browsing the wares on display, mine eyes were met with a relic from my past: a piece from the choral attire that I had discarded decades before, countless malms away.
I felt at once that it was not mere chance that had reunited me with it, and put forth the coin with nary a pause. Holding the garment in my hands, I resolved to find a worthy heir to my legacy.
Alas, no sooner had I arrived in the Twelveswood than I found myself mobbed by archers seeking to hone their skills. Amongst those who came, not a one showed the least interest in poetry and verse.
Sorely discouraged and regretting my decision, I made to strike camp and leave the Twelveswood once more, never to return.
It was then that you appeared, young one.
When you expressed your desire to learn song, I could scarce contain my joy.
Looking back, I am fully convinced that our meeting had been preordained.
Your coming has instilled me with the courage to attend that matter of which I spoke earlier.
I am ready─ready to make a pilgrimage to the scene of my regiment's demise.
Ever since that fateful day, I have been haunted by visions of my fallen comrades, torment graven upon their bloodied faces.
Lost to hope but too craven to end my own life, I wandered the land aimlessly, seeking a place to die. But the heavens denied me even that.
Yet just when it seemed that despair would draw me wholly into its black abyss, never to emerge again, a melody resounded within me.
It was then that I awakened to the power of song and found new purpose in life.
I embarked upon a journey to master such verses as would bestow peace upon the fallen, that I might lay the tortured souls of my comrades to rest.
It has taken long years, but now I believe I can offer a requiem worthy of my comrades. To do so, however, I require one last favor of you, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)].

I would have your company at the scene of my regiment's demise, where the Griffin Crossing meets the central highlands. The area teems with savage fiends, and my harp alone will yield little protection against their like.
With your help, I shall confront my inner demons and beg forgiveness of my comrades.
Oblige me this one wish, and the final piece of the choral attire shall be yours.
Words suffice not to express my gratitude. Your presence kindles within me a courage I had thought lost.
I would have none other by my side as I undertake this pilgrimage─now, as I enter the most daunting stage of my life.
Heed me, O Puissant Althyk! Reverse Thee the dance of the stars athwart the night sky, that we might ease the suffering of souls long departed!
O Puissant Althyk... Is it Thy will that my soul should never know peace?

Well would ye look at that, laddies―another fearless adventurer wanders into the forge. Ye like playin' Knights 'n' Dragons with the other kiddies, eh? We can play if ye like. Just let me warm me poker first.
Ah, so ye reckon ye've got iron in yer veins now, eh? Well, we'll jus' see about that, won't we? Tell us, what mangy moniker did yer mammy cry out when ye finally quit her quakin' loins?

Less than two suns past, I heard another report of a ship being sunk during a skirmish with the fishbacks. It's a bloody crime, it is. Never would've happened if that vessel had been properly fitted. Never.

Far too many captains are brought up believing every ship is destined to sink─counting down the days from the very morning of her launch.[@CR]Bollocks to that, I say! At least it would be if they could do something about that horrible heat... It's oft hotter in the streets there than it is here in our forges.

A sea voyage to Ul'dah? I consider myself fortunate that I don't have to join you. That place is two hells hotter than the seven we already have. Forgemasters left fer th' Coral Tower lookin' t' garner the Admiral's gratitude fer takin' on th' cannon order...an' perhaps a second chest o' gil fer a job well done.
But if ye ask me, they'll have been glad jus' t' put a few malms 'twixt them an' the forges. Can't say as I blames 'em, neither.
Ever wonder why, when ye drop 'em in the sea, a shipwright's steel don't sink like a smitty's iron does?
'Cause Llymlaen ain't no smitty!

Since we got a windwheel on most o' Limsa's ships, reports o' sinkin's have fallen faster'n a whore's undies─which would be all plums an' kisses, if the makin' o' said contraptions hadn't left the guild in such a sorry state. T' cut a long story short, blood be boilin' hotter than a midsummer noon's forge.

But ye not need worry yerself o'er such matters. Smoothin' things out 'twixt th' smitties an' wrights be [@1A(1)]my[@1A(0)] job─'tain't no concern o' yers if the task be harder'n climbin' Widow Cliffs wi' me teeth...thrice a bleedin' bell! Anyroad, while I gets on wi' doin' that, speak t' Mimidoa an' partake in a sprinklin' o' his knowledge. The dusty ol' bugger's been up there musin' fer th' past few days.

Oh, an' tell him Bodenolf says as we should take th' 'Cudas' coin an' make 'em all the bloody cannons they want. That way, when anyone asks, we can say 'twas none other than Naldiq an' Vymelli's what rid the world o' th' sirens!

There be sparks flyin' in th' forgemasters' alcove, an' they ain't comin' from the poundin' o' steel. No, th' two've been buttin' their leaden heads th' past fortnight o'er that thrice-damned order from th' 'Cudas. Since lavishin' all our supplies on the makin' of their bloody cannons, there ain't been near enough ore left t' shoe a one-legged chocobo, let alone build a ship, an' th' wrights is startin' t' fall behind on orders fer other clients.

Just wait! When ye be out on th' sea, all by yer lonesome, without so much as a speck of ore in yer pocket, ye'll curse yerself fer not havin' wits enough t' stock up at Joellaut's when ye had the chance. Don't say I didn't warn ye well!

The gall of them armorers to complain at a time like this! The title of senior forgemaster has fallen to a smitty, so it goes without saying that smitty projects'll take precedence over aught the shipwrights have planned. Same thing happened last season when [@1A(1)]their[@1A(0)] head was senior, and the same'll happen next season.
Just the way it is. Naught'll come of getting all unsettled.

The gall of them armorers to complain at a time like this! The title of senior forgemaster has fallen to a smitty, so it goes without saying that smitty projects'll take precedence over aught the shipwrights have planned. Same thing happened last season when [@1A(1)]their[@1A(0)] head was senior, and the same'll happen next season.
And if you don't like it, you know where the doors are.

Both smitties and shipwrights are swimming in a sea of pride broader than the Indigo Deep, and there'll be hoarfrost riming the Seventh Gate before either'll swallow enough of it to admit the other is even approaching as good as they are. Be that as it may, neither can they deny that the guild would be less than half what it is if either set was to bugger off.

Sadly, recent [@1A(1)]decisions[@1A(0)] by the acting forgemaster have rent a rift between us, and said ever-widening chasm is starting to affect our work. Yet even though there ain't a soul that cannot see the fix we're in, neither side's stepping forward to offer the other aught more than fusty jibes.

A smitty must [@1A(1)]attack[@1A(0)] 'is work in th' same manner a marauder attacks a ruttin' plague rat crawled out from 'neath a rock, savvy? So, won't none take [@1A(1)]offense[@1A(0)] at ye gettin' a bit zealous wi' that 'ammer o' yers.

Jus' make sure as ye don't go gettin' [@1A(1)]over[@1A(0)]-zealous, right? Them tactics may line yer pockets wi' gelt in a city o' gullible sods th' likes o' Gridania or Ul'dah, but all it'll earn ye in this den o' pirates is a rusty dirk in th' gut.

A smitty must [@1A(1)]attack[@1A(0)] 'is work in th' same manner a marauder attacks a ruttin' plague rat crawled out from 'neath a rock, savvy? So, won't none take [@1A(1)]offense[@1A(0)] at ye gettin' a bit zealous wi' that 'ammer o' yers.

Now, armorers, on tother 'and, is always [@1A(1)]defensive[@1A(0)] about aught 'n' everythin'. Why, their forgemaster once told us we was free t' throw at 'em whatsoe'er we pleased, be it our weapons or our words, for there weren't naught as could penetrate th' thick platin' o' their adamant wills. Ha!
What to do!? What to do!? The once-sporadic squabbling has become inconveniently incessant since our all-important ore supplies started to dwindle!
Oh, I pray this does not come to anything as barbaric as brawling. A conscientious craftsman must [@1A(1)]always[@1A(0)] take care to keep his hands from harm!
What to do!? What to do!? There's naught but tension 'twixt the guild's two ever-bickering branches!
Oh, I pray this does not come to anything as malapropos as mud-slinging, or, still more awful, ore-slinging! A deftly chucked chunk could well put out an onlooker's eye!
T' arms, [@IF($E9(4),lass,lad)]! Tonight we dines on siren!

Heh heh! Word's reached me good ear that them 'Cudas be plannin' a good ol' fashioned purge o' the outlyin' isles. Fixin' t' follow in the steps o' one Mistbeard, they be. Well, we can't go lettin' that happen. Got t' get there afore th' 'Cudas make a right mess o' things, an' a mess they'll make, oh aye. A bleedin' mess an' a half.

I'd sail meself there if I could, but lately me eyes been followin' in th' footsteps o' me ears, if me ears had feet─which they don't, mind. Anyroad, I needs meself a navigator, an' I ain't talkin' th' godly kind. Ain't afeared, now, are ye, [@IF($E9(4),lass,lad)]? Sirens don't have no power o'er a man so long as he cannot hear their sweet, sweet song.

An' that be where ol' Mimidoa can help ye, but only if ye help ol' Mimidoa first. Now, take this [@IF($E4($E8(1),1),[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000052,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,3,11000052,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)],[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000053,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,3,11000053,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)])] an' this recipe fer [@IF($E4($E8(1),1),[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000050,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,1,11000050,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)],[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000051,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,1,11000051,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)])], an' craft us one good 'n' quick. I'll do th' rest.

Takin' th' fight t' th' sirens!? Sounds like a lifetime poundin' the anvil's finally rattled the ol' bugger's thinker loose, an' ye've been listenin' t' th' sad sound of it rollin' around in his braincase.

Let me ask ye this, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]─how is it ye expect t' slay a gaggle o' mythical merbeasts when all ye've got in yer quiverin' hand is a bloomin' [@IF($E4($E8(1),1),cross-pein hammer,raisin' hammer)]?

I wish ye all the Spinner's luck, the Builder's craft, the Scholar's wits, and the Navigator's winds on yer journey. O' course, if ye'd so much as an onze o' th' Matron's sense, ye'd see the folly in this feckless venture o' yers an' stay here in Limsa.

But my bet is that ye've set yer mind on seein' matters through t' the end. Well, if that be th' case, then I only hope ye's got somethin' in that pack o' yers t' protect ye from th' sirens' song. A [@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000022,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,3,11000022,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)]'ll serve fer a passin' ship, but ye'll be paddlin' straight fer th' buggers' bandstand...

Aye, sailors are saying they can still hear the sirens' calls, but so far there ain't been any reports of sunken ships or crazy-eyed crews. Which is [@1A(1)]exactly[@1A(0)] why there ain't the merest hint of a bloody reason to go forging all those cannons in the hopes of culling mystical, magical monsters [@1A(1)]which[@1A(0)]─by dint of their miraculous return after certain extinction─have proven beyond all doubt to be invincible merbeasts from the depths of the seven hells, come to make thralls of us all! You cannot kill what cannot die, I tell you!
The only thing Limsa [@1A(1)]truly[@1A(0)] needs is some good, fast ships to make sure that if any poor bugger ever gets too close, they can be long gone before their ears know what's tickled them.
I've had enough! My head feels as if it were about to explode!

What I [@1A(1)]need[@1A(0)] is some time away from the heat of the forges. A distant island where I could take in the sun, the wind, and the salt of the sea. Where I could listen to the sweet songs of a silky-tongued bard as I supped on suckling pig and a tall cup of sweet red. <sigh>

Eh!? Waitin' fer th' [@IF($E4($E8(1),1),[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000050,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,3,11000050,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)],[@SWITCH([@SHEET(itemData,11000051,41)],[@COLOR(#fff3f3f3)],[@COLOR(#ffc0ffa0)],[@COLOR(#ff60c8ff)],[@COLOR(#ffb38cff)],[@COLOR(#ffffa666)],[@COLOR(#ffe5dd7e)])][@EDGECOLOR(#ff262626)][@SHEETEN(xtx/itemName,3,11000051,1,1)][@EDGECOLOR($EC)][@COLOR($EC)])] t' craft itself, are ye, [@IF($E9(4),lass,lad)]? Heh heh.
Me forgemates seem right chipper these days...
Might be it has somethin' t' do with that moot they called while I was at home tendin' me sprat when he come down with th' Rot.
Pounded some sense into them sirens, I hear. 'Tis a fine thing ye did fer th' city. A fine thing, indeed.
But 'tis an even finer thing ye did fer us armorers. Now, might be as we have enough ore t' start workin' on buildin' ships once more.
Mimidoa's told th' forgemasters th' city won't be experiencin' any more problems with th' sirens.
Still boggles me mind how a fledglin' forgelin' an' a shriveled ol' coot with a knackered ear pacified a bloody army o' wanton wenches...but some scenes don't bear thinkin' about.
How in th' seven hells did ye─ But I thought─ There can't be─ Oh, bugger it! I've rivets t' pound.

An' our champion's returned from [@IF($E9(4),her,his)] noble quest! Did ye slay the evil dragon an' [@IF($E9(4),spare th' handsome prince an embarrassin' defeat,rescue the fair maiden from her tower)]? An' were ye rewarded fer yer just deeds with a purse full o' gold an' pearls? Eh? Ye were!? Then what better place t' spend yer newly won riches than here!?
While you and Mimidoa were away, I heeded my own advice and found a nice little island near the Cieldalaes where I could sing and dance and revel in the moonlight. It was quite refreshing.
I even met a handsome smitty there one night. And who knows─if he shows me he can handle his tool right, I may one day grant him leave to temper his blade in my forge.
Now that business with the sirens is behind us, maybe the smitties and the wrights can get back to working together.
And [@1A(1)]you[@1A(0)] can get back to the forge, where you belong. You'll make a fine crafter yet, [@SPLIT([@STRING($EB(1))], ,1)]─of that there ain't no doubt.

Both our forgemasters be stubborn as rocks an' cold as steel. That bein' so, they don't take kindly t' their smitties an' wrights sneakin' off to no island fer a drop o' wine 'n' whatever when there's still fire in the forges.
Trouble is, ain't none as can remember the forges bein' dark since afore ol' Naldiq lit th' first one back in the day.
<gulp> Mimidoa will have our heads!
Now that he knows our secret, no smitty nor shipwright will be safe!
<sigh> Mimidoa will have our sanity!
Now that he's silenced the sirens' song, no shipwright nor smitty will know a moment's calm!
City saw rumors o' th' sirens die down fer a spell, but now th' 'Cudas be fixin' t' send a ship out t' find th' serenadin' strumpets an' riddle 'em wi' lead.
Long as they go 'quipped wi' them cannons we forged 'em, I rate they'll knock th' wind out th' vocalizin' vixens afore their melodies start messin' with th' men's minds.
But ol' Mimidoa don't reckon on it bein' so simple─an' he ain't often wrong. Add to that, this whole mess has got th' smitties an' armorers proper clawin' at each other's throats...er, more'n usual.

Sharp 'venturer like yerself more'n like sussed out that ol' Mimidoa lost th' workin's in his right ear durin' the last purge o' th' sirens. That bein' so, when he says he's got a “feelin'” about the 'Cudas' plans, I reckon it best we lends him [@1A(1)]our[@1A(0)] right ears, if ye catch me drift.

'Tain't never wise t' go turnin' a deaf─er, t' go disregardin' ol' Mimidoa when he's talkin' o' trouble. Pay no heed t' th' billowin' storm clouds on th' horizon, yer bones're bound t' get soaked, savvy?
